Notes · VFX

Making liquid read as metal

A liquid simulation is usually judged by whether it moves correctly. That is the easy half. The hard half is whether it reads as the material you claimed it was once it is lit, composited and four seconds long on a screen. These are the notes from building Molten Flow as a lighting study first and a simulation second.

The surface is the character, not the motion

Two simulations can share the same velocity field and still look like different substances. What separates water from oil from molten metal is mostly what happens in the top fraction of a millimetre: how the surface holds a highlight, how it breaks into beads, how it drags when it stretches. Get those right and the motion can be simple. Get them wrong and no amount of turbulence will convince anyone.

That inverts the usual order. It is tempting to start with the solver settings and adjust until it "looks good". It is faster to decide the material first — what temperature, what thickness, what oxidation — and then to keep only the solver settings that serve that decision.

Viscosity is a storytelling choice

Viscosity is not a physical constant in a film context; it is a pace control. A thick, slow material reads as heavy and hot and dangerous. A thin one reads as spilled and careless. The same event — metal pouring into a channel — means something different depending on which one you shoot.

  • Thick and slow: reads as industrial, molten, expensive. Good for scale and threat.
  • Thin and fast: reads as watery, accidental, urgent. Good for a moment of loss of control.
  • Variable by region: the most interesting option — a skin that cools at the edges while the core stays bright.

Light does most of the work

A molten material is, physically, an emissive object with a very high dynamic range. That means the render problem is closer to lighting a practical lamp than to shading a normal surface. It blows out where it is hottest and goes almost black where it has cooled, and the transition between those two states is where the material is legible.

The practical consequence: exposure is a creative decision, not a correction. Pulling exposure down to protect the highlights loses the glow that tells the viewer it is hot. Letting it clip in the core and holding the detail in the cooled edges is usually the better trade.

Reading it at four seconds

A study like this is not watched for its plot. It is watched for one or two beats: the pour, the splash, the settle. Anything that does not contribute to those beats is noise, however technically impressive it is.

That is worth stating before the simulation is built, because it decides the resolution, the frame range and the camera. A four-second clip does not need a solver that survives a ten-minute sequence; it needs one that looks right for four seconds at a specific angle.

The project

Molten Flow is a liquid and molten-material study — viscosity, surface tension and how the material reads against light, built to be lit rather than simply simulated.
